title: Eating in… and out
summary: Talk about habits and things happening now. Learn food and cooking words.

blocks.p: Use the present simple for things that are always or generally true, and for things that happen regularly. Add -s / -es with he, she and it. Use do / does to make questions and negatives.
ex: I usually have toast and coffee in the morning.
My brother doesn't eat meat.
How often do you eat out?

blocks.p: Words like always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never go before the main verb but after the verb be. Longer expressions like every day or twice a week usually go at the end.
ex: She never cooks on Mondays.
I'm always hungry in the evening.
We get a takeaway every Friday.

blocks.h: Present continuous: now and around now
blocks.p: Use the present continuous (am / is / are + verb-ing) for actions in progress at the moment of speaking, or temporary situations around now.
ex: Can I call you back? I'm cooking dinner.
The price of olive oil is rising at the moment.
Is your sister still working at that café?

blocks.p: Remember QUASI: Question word, Auxiliary, Subject, Infinitive.
ex: What time does the restaurant open?
Where are you having lunch today?

blocks.p: Some verbs describe states, feelings, opinions or the senses, not actions. We don't normally use them in the continuous form, even when we mean 'now'. Common ones: be, believe, belong, depend, hate, know, like, love, mean, need, prefer, realize, remember, seem, want, and the senses look, smell, taste, sound.
ex: I need a coffee right now.
This soup tastes amazing.
Do you know this restaurant?

blocks.p: A few verbs can be actions or states, with a different meaning. have: have lunch (action) vs. have a car (possession). think: think about something (action) vs. think that… (opinion).
ex: Sorry, I'm having a shower. I'll call you later.
My parents have a small flat by the sea.
What are you thinking about?
I think this café makes the best coffee in town.

a long green vegetable like a small cucumber (AmE: zucchini)
a sweet tropical fruit with orange flesh
a red vegetable, sweet and hollow inside
cooked in the oven, without oil (bread, cakes, potatoes)
cooked in hot oil in a pan
cooked under or over direct heat
cooked in the oven, usually with some oil (meat, potatoes)
cooked over boiling water, in the steam
eat in a restaurant, not at home
eat or drink less of something

blocks.p: English has short and long versions of some vowels. The long ones have the symbol ː. Making the vowel the right length can change the word.
ex: ship, sheep
full, fool

title: Modern families
summary: Talk about the future in three ways. Describe family members and personalities.

sections.title: Future forms: going to, present continuous, will / won't

blocks.h: be going to: plans and evidence
blocks.p: Use be going to + infinitive for things you have already decided to do, and for predictions when you can see evidence now.
ex: I'm going to learn to cook Thai food this year.
Look at the traffic! We're going to be late.
We aren't going to travel abroad this summer.

blocks.p: Use the present continuous for future arrangements: plans with a time, a place, other people, a ticket or a booking. It's very common with travel verbs: go, come, leave, arrive.
ex: My cousins are coming to stay next weekend.
I'm meeting my lawyer at ten tomorrow.
Dad is flying to Madrid on Monday and coming home on Thursday.

blocks.h: will / won't: instant decisions, promises, offers, predictions
blocks.p: Use will / won't when you decide at the moment of speaking, and for promises, offers and predictions (often with I think…).
ex: Someone's at the door. I'll open it.
I'll pay you back tomorrow. I promise.
I think you'll enjoy this book.

blocks.p: Use Shall I…? to offer help and Shall we…? to make suggestions.
ex: Shall I carry those bags for you?
Shall we order a pizza tonight?

items: your father's wife, who is not your mother

groups.note: un-, dis- and in- make opposites. in- becomes im- before b, m, p; ir- before r; il- before l.

blocks.p: In words with two or more syllables, one syllable is stronger. Dictionaries mark it with ˈ before the stressed syllable. Prefixes like un- and in- are not usually stressed.
ex: ambitious /æmˈbɪʃəs/
reliable /rɪˈlaɪəbl/
competitive /kəmˈpetətɪv/
sociable /ˈsəʊʃəbl/

blocks.p: We stress the words that carry the meaning (nouns, main verbs, adjectives) and say small words like to, a, are, will quickly and weakly.
ex: We're going to have a party.
I'll call you tomorrow.

grammar.e: A decision already made → be going to.

title: Practical English 1: Reacting to what people say
summary: Show interest and emotion when someone tells you news.

blocks.p: In conversation, good listeners react. Choose the phrase that matches the news.
table: You're kidding! / No way! / You're joking!
That's great news! / How fantastic! / Congratulations!
Oh no! / I'm so sorry. / What a pity! / How awful!

blocks.p: Two useful patterns: How + adjective! and What (a) + noun! Use a / an with singular countable nouns.
ex: How amazing!
How awful!
What a pity!
What a good idea!
What terrible news!

blocks.p: Sound interested: your voice should go up and down a lot. A flat voice sounds bored or rude.
ex: Really? That's great news!
Oh no! I'm so sorry.

A: My flight was cancelled. B: ___
A: Tom is getting married next week! B: ___ He told me he never wanted to marry!
A: I've lost my wallet with all my cards. B: ___
A: Did you know octopuses have three hearts? B: ___

title: Spending money
summary: Choose between the present perfect and the past simple. Talk about money.

blocks.h: Present perfect: have / has + past participle
blocks.p: Use the present perfect when the time is not important or not finished: experiences in your life (often with ever / never), and recent actions with a result now (often with just).
ex: Have you ever forgotten your PIN?
I've never had a credit card.
Oh no! I've just dropped my phone in the sink.

blocks.p: already (= sooner than expected) goes before the main verb in positive sentences. yet goes at the end of negatives and questions.
ex: I've already booked the tickets.
The bank hasn't answered my email yet.
Have you opened your new account yet?

blocks.p: Use the past simple when you say or ask when something happened, or the time is clearly finished: yesterday, last year, in 2019, two days ago, when I was a child.
ex: I bought these boots in the sales last January.
When did you open your bank account?
We didn't go on holiday last year.

blocks.p: We often start with the present perfect (the general experience) and continue with the past simple (the details).
ex: Have you ever been to Japan? Yes, I have. I went there in 2018.
I've lost my keys. I left them on the bus this morning.

items: take money from someone and give it back later (borrow FROM)
give money to someone for a time (lend TO)
need to pay back money you borrowed: I owe you €20

don't have enough money to buy something
ask a price for a service: They charged me €60
have a price: These shoes cost $200
have a certain value: My car is worth €5,000

put money into a business or property to make a profit
collect money for a good cause
a paper that shows how much you must pay
the money you have and your plan for spending it
paying by holding your card or phone near a reader
you pay a company and they pay if something bad happens
money that you borrow from a bank
a loan to buy a house or flat
the money you get every month for your job
money that you pay to the government
Can I pay by card? / I'll pay in cash.

blocks.p: The letter o has several sounds. The most common are /ɒ/ (short), /əʊ/ (like 'go') and /ʌ/ (like 'up').
ex: money
honest
loan

blocks.p: When or is stressed it's usually /ɔː/: afford, mortgage, order. But after w it's usually /ɜː/: work, worth, world.
ex: afford
mortgage
worth
work

title: Changing lives
summary: Say how long something has lasted with for / since. Use strong adjectives.

sections.title: Present perfect + for / since; present perfect continuous

blocks.p: To talk about a situation that started in the past and continues now, use the present perfect, not the present simple. Use for + a period of time and since + a point in time.
ex: I've had this bike for six years.
My aunt has lived in Cork since 2015.
How long have you lived here?

blocks.p: for: two weeks, ten years, a long time, ages. since: Monday, 2010, June, I was a child, last summer.
ex: for three months
since last Christmas
since I was at university

blocks.h: Present perfect continuous: have / has been + verb-ing
blocks.p: With action verbs we often use the present perfect continuous with for / since / How long to emphasize the activity continuing up to now. With non-action verbs (know, have = possess, be, like) use the present perfect simple.
ex: How long have you been saving for the trip?
The baby has been crying since six o'clock.
We've known each other since primary school.

blocks.h: Recent activities with a present result
blocks.p: We also use the continuous for an activity that has just stopped and explains what we see now.
ex: You're out of breath. Have you been running?
Yes, I've been jogging in the park.

blocks.p: With live and work both forms are fine with for / since.
ex: I've worked here since 2019.
I've been working here since 2019.

groups.note: Strong adjectives already mean 'very ___'. Use absolutely or really with them, NOT very: absolutely exhausted, NOT very exhausted.

blocks.p: In questions with How long have you been…?, the important words are stressed and have you been is said very fast: /əv jə bɪn/.
ex: How long have you been studying?
How long have you known her?

blocks.p: We often give strong adjectives extra stress to show emotion.
ex: I'm absolutely exhausted!
The water was freezing!
I'm starving!

grammar.q: I ___ here since 2018.
grammar.e: Started in the past and continues → present perfect, not present simple.

grammar.q: I've had this laptop ___ three years.
He's been in hospital ___ Monday.
How long ___ your best friend?
grammar.e: know is non-action → present perfect simple.

grammar.q: It ___ all day. Take an umbrella.
grammar.e: Action continuing up to now → present perfect continuous.

grammar.q: Why are you so dirty? What ___?
grammar.e: Recent activity with a visible result.

How long have you ___ (wait) for the bus? Use the continuous.

Complete with for or since: I haven't seen him ___ ages.
Complete with for or since: My dad has worked for the same company ___ he left university.
grammar.e: since + a point in time (a clause).

vocabulary.e: absolutely + strong adjective; very + normal adjective.

vocabulary.q: A: Are you scared of flying? B: I'm ___! I never fly.

title: Survive the drive
summary: Compare things with comparatives and superlatives. Talk about transport and journeys.

blocks.p: Short adjectives add -er (old → older, big → bigger, easy → easier). Long adjectives use more / less (more expensive). Irregular: good → better, bad → worse, far → further.
ex: The tram is faster than the bus.
Dublin is more expensive than Limerick.
Driving here is less stressful than in Madrid.

blocks.p: Use as + adjective + as to say two things are equal, and not as … as to say one is less.
ex: The coach isn't as comfortable as the train.
A taxi is as quick as the Underground at night.

blocks.h: Object pronouns after than and as
blocks.p: After than and as, use an object pronoun (me, him, us) or subject + verb. Use the same as for two identical things.
ex: My son is taller than me.
My son is taller than I am.
Your scooter is the same as mine.

blocks.p: Adverbs compare the same way: fast → faster, slowly → more slowly, well → better, badly → worse.
ex: My brother cycles faster than me.
Lorries drive more slowly than cars.
I don't drive as well as my wife.

blocks.p: Use the superlative to compare one thing with the whole group. Use the and often in (in the world, in my family) or a present perfect (the best film I've ever seen).
ex: What's the cheapest way to get to the airport?
It's the busiest motorway in the country.
That was the longest journey I've ever made.

items: a comfortable bus for long journeys
a boat that carries people and cars across water
a big vehicle that carries goods (AmE: truck)
a small motorbike, or an electric one you stand on
an electric vehicle that runs on rails in the street
trains under the city, e.g. in London (AmE: subway)
a vehicle for carrying goods, smaller than a lorry
a big, fast road between cities (AmE: freeway)
the belt that keeps you safe in your seat

a long line of cars that can't move

the time when everyone travels to or from work
a place with white stripes where people cross the road
part of the road only for bicycles
a place to buy fuel (AmE: gas station)
repairs being done to a road
start a journey: We set off at 7.00.
collect someone in a car (opposite: drop off)
finally arrive somewhere you didn't plan
have no more of something: We've run out of petrol.

groups.note: Use take + time to talk about how long a journey lasts.
items: It takes an hour to get there.
It took me two hours to get home yesterday.
How long does it take you to get to work?

blocks.p: /ʃ/ as in shower (just air), /tʃ/ as in chair (a short 't' + sh), /dʒ/ as in jazz (the voiced version of /tʃ/).
ex: crash
catch
journey

blocks.p: In fast speech, words join together: a final consonant links to a vowel (the most_interesting); the same consonant joins into one (the worst_time); /t/ or /d/ + /t/ or /d/ often joins (the biggest_danger).
ex: It's the most interesting city.
That was the worst time of day.
Speed is the biggest danger.

grammar.e: After than: object pronoun (or 'than I am').

title: Men, women, and children
summary: Use a / an, the, and no article correctly. Learn verbs and adjectives with prepositions.

sections.title: Articles: a / an, the, no article

blocks.p: Use a / an with singular countable nouns: to say what something is or what someone does (jobs), the first time you mention something, in exclamations with What…!, and in frequency expressions.
ex: My neighbour is a pilot.
I found a wallet in the street.
What a beautiful view!
I have Spanish lessons twice a week.

blocks.p: Use the when you mention something again, when it's clear which one, when there is only one, with places in a town (the cinema, the theatre), and with superlatives.
ex: I found a wallet in the street. The wallet was empty.
Can you pass me the salt?
The sun rises in the east.
It's the oldest bridge in the city.

blocks.p: Don't use an article when you speak in general with plural or uncountable nouns; with home, work, school, church, bed after at / to / from; with meals; and with next / last + week, month, etc.
ex: Cats sleep a lot.
Health is more important than money.
My husband is at work.
We usually have lunch at one.
I'm starting a new course next month.

blocks.p: Compare: I like dogs (all dogs, in general) vs. I don't like the dogs next door (specific dogs).
ex: I like dogs.
I don't like the dogs next door.

items: arrive in a city / arrive at a place
arrive in Milan; arrive at the airport

groups.note: After a preposition, use the -ing form: I'm excited about going to Brazil.
items: emotionally near: I'm close to my sister.

blocks.p: The schwa is the most common sound in English. Most unstressed small words use it: a, of, to, for, than, at.
ex: a cup of tea
Girls are better at reading than boys.

blocks.p: Say /ðə/ before a consonant sound and /ði/ before a vowel sound. It's the sound that matters, not the letter: the university /ðə/, the hour /ði/.
ex: the man
the woman
the end
the internet

title: Practical English 2: Giving opinions
summary: Give your opinion, agree and disagree politely.

table: I think… / I don't think… / Personally, I think… / In my opinion,… / If you ask me,…
I agree. / I totally agree. / Exactly. / That's true.
That's true, but… / I see what you mean, but… / I'm not sure.
I don't agree. / I don't think that's true. / I'm not sure about that.
blocks.p: Use I don't think + positive verb, not I think + negative: I don't think it's a good idea (more natural than I think it isn't a good idea).
Listen to how the speakers soften disagreement.
ex: In my opinion, Dublin is the friendliest city in Europe.
I see what you mean, but it's too expensive for me.
Personally, I think working from home is better.
I totally agree.

blocks.p: Some words are different: mobile phone (BrE) / cell phone (AmE); flat / apartment; lift / elevator; the Underground / the subway.

A: Cycling is dangerous. B: ___, but it's also very healthy.

o: I see what you mean, but…

phrases.q: The American word for 'mobile phone' is…
Complete: ___ ask me, the city is too expensive.

title: Bad manners?
summary: Talk about rules, obligation and advice. Learn phone language.

sections.title: Obligation and prohibition: have to, must, should

blocks.p: Both mean it's necessary. have to is more common for general rules and laws; must often expresses what the speaker personally feels is necessary, and is common in written rules. Both can also be used for strong recommendations.
ex: In Ireland, you have to drive on the left.
I must remember to buy milk.
You must try this cake. It's delicious!

blocks.p: must only exists in the present. For the past, future and other forms, use have to: had to, will have to, have had to. Questions and negatives use do / does / did.
ex: I had to work late yesterday.
Does your son have to wear a uniform?
You'll have to wait.

blocks.p: These are completely different! don't have to = it's not necessary (you can if you want). mustn't = it's prohibited, don't do it. You can also use can't or not allowed to for prohibition.
ex: You don't have to bring anything. We have lots of food.
You mustn't touch the paintings.
You can't smoke in restaurants.

blocks.p: Use should to give advice or say what you think is right. It's weaker than must. ought to means the same as should.
ex: You should see a doctor about that cough.
You shouldn't go to bed so late.
I think schools should teach more languages.
You ought to apologize to her.

blocks.p: Many English words have letters that are not pronounced. Common patterns: k before n (knife, know), w before r (write, wrong), l in -alk / -alf / -ould (walk, half, should), t in -sten / -stle (listen, castle), gh (ought, light), h at the start of some words (hour, honest).
ex: We swam round the whole island.
Listen! I can hear someone talking.
You should know the answer.
The bus ought to come in half an hour.

title: Yes, I can!
summary: Talk about ability and possibility. Use -ed and -ing adjectives.

sections.title: Ability and possibility: can, could, be able to

blocks.p: can = present ability or possibility. could = general ability in the past. They are modal verbs: no -s, no 'to', no other tenses.
ex: I can't find my keys anywhere.
My grandfather could speak four languages.
We couldn't see the stage from our seats.

blocks.h: be able to: all the other forms
blocks.p: For forms that can doesn't have (infinitive, -ing, present perfect, future), use be able to + infinitive.
ex: I'd love to be able to play the piano.
I haven't been able to sleep well this week.
Next year you'll be able to drive.
I love being able to walk to work.

blocks.p: In the present and past, be able to is possible but sounds more formal than can / could. For one specific success in the past, we often use was / were able to (or managed to).
ex: We are able to offer you the job.
After two hours, we were able to fix the car.

blocks.p: can has no future or infinitive: NOT I will can, NOT I want to can. Say I'll be able to, I want to be able to.

groups.note: -ed describes how a person feels: I'm bored. -ing describes the thing or person that causes the feeling: The film is boring.
items: a bit angry / making you a bit angry
sad because it wasn't as good as expected
feeling stupid in front of others
annoyed because you can't do something
needing rest / making you need rest

blocks.p: In positive sentences, can is usually unstressed: /kən/. can't is always stressed: /kɑːnt/ in British English. In short answers, can is strong: /kæn/.
ex: I can swim.
I can't swim.
Yes, I can.

blocks.p: The stress doesn't move when you add -ed or -ing.
ex: embarrassing /ɪmˈbærəsɪŋ/
frustrated /frʌˈstreɪtɪd/
disappointing /ˌdɪsəˈpɔɪntɪŋ/
